Теория, измерение и экономическое значение
Author: Аванесян Карен Алексеевич
Institution: Южный Федеральный Университет
Year: 2025
Language: Russian
A comprehensive academic presentation exploring the theoretical foundations, measurement approaches, and economic significance of non-cognitive skills in human capital theory. The presentation covers the evolution from traditional cognitive-focused models to contemporary frameworks incorporating personality traits, behavioral patterns, and socio-emotional competencies.
Key topics covered: - Conceptualization challenges and terminological debates - The Big Five personality model (OCEAN) and alternative frameworks - Empirical evidence from international and Russian labor market studies - Policy implications for educational systems and skill development programs - Future research directions in the field

title: Media
text:
This page contains links to the media that referenced my research reports produced during the COVID-19 pandemic using real-time data collected through open sources and internal monitoring platforms.

Associated Press, September 2021
   Empty desk array at UN spotlights lost learning in pandemic
UNITED NATIONS (AP) — While world leaders converge on the U.N. headquarters next week, the coronavirus will be on the agenda — and a set of empty, backpack-draped chairs and desks will symbolize what the pandemic has done to education.



CBS News, March 3, 2021
   U.N. uses empty desks of “Pandemic Classroom” in call on nations to end “very worrying” COVID school closures
United Nations — The coronavirus has claimed more than 2.5 million lives and infected almost 115 million people globally, but it’s having a far wider impact on almost all of the world’s children. The United Nations is trying to highlight the damage done by widespread school closures by giving it visual representation on the grounds of U.N. headquarters in New York, and urging countries to reopen classrooms.



Washington Post, March 2021
   U.N. warns of ‘education emergency’ as millions miss school because of covid-19 closures
More than 168 million children around the world have missed school for nearly a year because of coronavirus restrictions, the United Nations Children’s Fund said Wednesday.
UNICEF described the impact the shutdowns have had on school-age children as a “catastrophic education emergency” with “devastating consequences for children’s learning and well-being.”



UN News, March 2021
   Over 168 million children miss nearly a year of schooling, UNICEF says
UNICEF unveiled ‘Pandemic Classroom’, a model classroom made up of 168 empty desks, each desk representing one million of the children living in countries where schools have been almost entirely closed, as a “solemn reminder of the classrooms in every corner of the world that remain empty”, said the agency.



Washington Post, August 2020
   At least 463 million students around the world have no access to digital or broadcast lessons, UNICEF report says
At least 463 million students around the world have no access to remote lessons provided by digital or broadcast means because families don’t have the ability to receive them or governments are not providing them, a new UNICEF report released Wednesday says.



Tableau Resources Blog, June 2020
   How UNICEF is using data to ensure global COVID-19 school closures don’t set kids back
COVID-19 is challenging nearly every community and every system in place across the world. For UNICEF, the UN’s organization focused on the rights and wellbeing of children everywhere, the pandemic poses a unique threat to children and families. On top of the economic instability that COVID-19 has brought to millions of families across the world, many of the systems in place that care for children and support their well-being have been impacted.

title: Каузальный анализ в R на данных RLMS-HSE
text:
Курс отвечает на один вопрос: как по наблюдательным данным оценить причинный эффект и не обмануть себя. Формулы сведены к минимуму (нотация потенциальных исходов), упор — на дизайн исследования, код в R и интерпретацию. Все примеры — на данных RLMS-HSE, российского лонгитюдного мониторинга домохозяйств.
Каждое занятие (≈90 минут): 20 минут «что это и в чём смысл», 50 минут живого кода на RLMS, 20 минут «как ошибаются» и мини-задача.


Одни и те же вопросы решаются на протяжении курса разными методами, чтобы была видна «лестница оценок» одного эффекта:

Образование → зарплата: OLS → мэтчинг → IPW/AIPW → FE → IV → модель Хекмана → медиация → causal forest → чувствительность.
Рождение ребёнка → занятость женщин: event study → DiD по материнскому капиталу → RD → IV Ангриста–Эванса → гетерогенность.




Пенсионная реформа 2019 (когортное повышение возраста), порог пенсионного возраста 55/60, пол первых двух детей (Ангрист–Эванс); материнский капитал 2007 — как пример, где DiD не проходит проверку предтрендов. Антитабачный закон и региональные ограничения алкоголя предложены как темы проектов.

text:
Как пользоваться
Слайды открываются по ссылкам в таблице (reveal.js: стрелки — навигация, Esc — обзор, S — заметки лектора, ? — все клавиши). Исходники лекций — файлы .qmd в папке causal-r/lectures/; каждая лекция самодостаточна: source("causal-r/R/load_panel.R") в начале подгружает панель, пакеты и оформление.

title: Каузальный анализ в R на данных RLMS-HSE
text:
Данные
Данные RLMS-HSE студенты скачивают самостоятельно после регистрации на сайте проекта; их редистрибуция запрещена. Курс даёт скрипты: R/01_extract_rlms.R извлекает нужные столбцы из объединённого файла индивидов (и детей по файлу родственников), R/02_recode_panel.R чистит коды и строит аналитические переменные, R/build_rlms_panel.R запускает оба шага, R/load_panel.R подгружает панель в каждой лекции. Переменные панели описаны в лекции 0.

Hello! I’m a Data Scientist at the Data & Analytics division of the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), where I build automated data pipelines, engineer reproducible workflows, and produce robust estimates that help countries track their progress toward child-related Sustainable Development Goals. My work sits at the intersection of data engineering and applied economic research — bringing together complex data systems to make evidence transparent and actionable.
Beyond my work at UNICEF, my academic portfolio focuses on human capital research, particularly how socio-emotional skills shape young people’s transitions from school to work. I study how these skills interact with education, labor market outcomes, and broader socio-economic inequalities, with a special focus on youth in developing and transition economies.
I strongly believe that doing statistical analysis should go beyond numbers and data points; it’s about understanding the stories these numbers tell and the lives they touch.

unicefData is an open data and analytics toolkit led by UNICEF’s Office of the Chief Statistician. It gives R, Python and Stata users a consistent interface to the UNICEF Data Warehouse over the SDMX API: automatic pagination, caching, country name lookups, metadata vintages, and full coverage of the child-related SDG indicators.

title: Software
text:
unequal (R package)
unequal measures inequality and decomposes it by population subgroup, income source, regression terms and over time, with every estimator tied to the equation it implements and competing methods offered side by side. It covers the Gini family and generalized entropy indices, Lorenz and concentration curves, Lorenz dominance tests, Kuznets curves, tax progressivity and redistribution, mobility, poverty (FGT, Watts, Sen, growth and redistribution decompositions), relative deprivation, inequality of opportunity, concentration indices for health outcomes, estimation from grouped data, and inference by bootstrap, jackknife and linearisation with complex survey designs.
Role: author and maintainer. Development version, not yet on CRAN.
Guide (PDF) Inequality analysis with the unequal package: a guide for economists and sociologists, 40+ pages with worked examples on a household survey.

United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), New York, USA

Working in Data & Analytics Section, helping countries to foster child well-being through data-driven insights, harnessing the power of analytics to support and enhance global child welfare initiatives.



Automated the process for generating statistical country briefs in R, utilizing Git/GitHub, to enable effective monitoring of progress on child-related Sustainable Development Goal indicators.


Optimized the ETL process between statistical estimates production and the UNICEF Data Warehouse by utilizing R and Python, significantly improving data consolidation and accessibility.


Co-led the technical team for the UNICEF Report on Progress on Children’s Wellbeing, taking a leading role in enhancing methodological rigor and broadening statistical analysis based on the principles of literate programming in R.


Led the UNICEF Report on Bridging the Digital Gender Divide, leveraging large-scale data and advanced statistical methods, including mixed-effect models, to advocate for equitable programs in digital skill acquisition.


Standardized complex survey data through data harmonization and using version control (Git and GitHub), improving the production of child well-being estimates.


Supervised a team of 3 analysts in the development of analytical tools to collect data on quality of learning amongst children.

United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), New York, USA


August 2019 — June 2022


Was working in the Education Data Unit of Data & Analytics Section.



Spearheaded the use of real time-data during COVID-19 emergency response for UNICEF’s Data & Analytics, using open-source and internally collected data to analyze socio-economic impact of the pandemic on child wellbeing.


Led the production of key data-driven reports on remote learning coverage, digital connectivity, and school closures, which influenced governmental policies and UNICEF country programs.


Developed innovative statistical methodologies like the ‘Remote Learning Readiness Index’ and the ‘Reachability Indicator’, that set up UNICEF internal monitoring and program work in developing countries during the COVID-19.


Co-led the MICS-EAGLE initiative to enhance the utilization of household survey data in developing countries for sector planning.


Built statistical/data analytic capacity using R, Stata, and SPSS, across international offices and ministries, facilitating better data management during emergency responses.

United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), Vienna, Austria


January 2019 — August 2019

Led the data analysis for the UNODC Global Study on Homicide 2019, authoring significant sections, creating foundational analytical methods, and producing homicide estimates.


Developed a Shiny R app for visualizing homicide data, integrating Plotly visualizations and Leaflet maps to effectively uncover and illustrate critical patterns and trends in homicide distribution.


Conducted comprehensive statistical forecasting and predictive modeling of time-series data on homicide trends.


Managed extensive databases using R and SQL, integrating geospatial and crime data for a holistic view of global homicide trends.


Created dynamic visualizations and web applications in R and Python to make complex data more accessible, aiding global decision-making.

International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Vienna, Austria


October 2015 — December 2018


Was working as a conference clerk and consultant to maintain conference participation data for different departments of the IAEA.



Enhanced the statistical reporting system for the Conference Services Section, improving data precision and operational efficiency.


Contributed to optimization of the IAEA Conferences and Events mobile application, significantly boosting user engagement.


Developed visualization and reporting tools for conference participation data, yielding insights into participant demographics and trends.
